title: Declaration Detectives
sub: Grades 3–4 · A Copy of a Copy

hero.credit: John Dunlap, printer, Philadelphia, 1776. Library of Congress, Rare Book and Special Collections Division. Public domain.

objective: Students will examine four copies of the Declaration of Independence as the exhibition’s *A Copy of a Copy* room shows them: the first printing of July 1776, the first printing with the signers’ names, Stone’s engraving of 1823 and the faded parchment today. They will find a clue on each, put the copies and the dates in order, and learn that the picture most people know is a copy of a copy.

materials: The *Show your class* page (page 3), projected; differentiated handouts, one per student
A magnifying glass or a paper “lens” for each group, if you have them
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** in *A Copy of a Copy*, open the case and solve each mission with the lens. When a clue is found, the room tells how that copy was made. Then try *Put Your Name to It*, and sign the Declaration under the signers.

steps.title: Is this the real thing?
script: Project Stone’s engraving with no caption. Ask: *“Is this the Declaration of Independence? What clues could tell you?”* Take ideas: the date at the top, the signatures, how clean and dark it looks. Then reveal: it is an **engraving made in 1823**, almost fifty years later. *“The picture almost everyone knows is a copy. Today you are detectives: which copy is which, and how close is each one to the real thing?”*

steps.title: Four copies
script: Show the four copies on page 3 in order. The **Dunlap broadside** was printed on the night of July 4 and the morning of July 5, 1776: about 200 copies, sent to governments, army commanders and the British Crown in London, and 26 survive. The **Goddard broadside** of 1777 was the first printing with the signers’ names, printed by Mary Katharine Goddard in Baltimore. **Stone’s engraving** was made in 1823 because the parchment was already showing its age. And the **signed parchment** itself is in the National Archives, faded almost away.

items.caption: The Dunlap broadside
items.alt: The Dunlap broadside: a single printed sheet headed “In Congress, July 4, 1776. A Declaration by the Representatives of the United States of America, in General Congress assembled,” with only John Hancock’s and Charles Thomson’s names printed at its foot

items.caption: The Goddard broadside
items.alt: The Goddard broadside: a printed sheet headed “In Congress, July 4, 1776. The Unanimous Declaration of the Thirteen United States of America,” the text in two columns, and below it the signers’ names in print, grouped by state

items.caption: Stone’s engraving
items.alt: William J. Stone’s engraving: the Declaration in crisp black lines on white, the whole text in a flowing hand, and every signature clear and dark at the foot, John Hancock’s largest

items.caption: The signed parchment today
items.alt: The signed parchment of the Declaration as it is today: a pale, worn sheet, its heading still dark, but most of its handwriting and nearly all the signatures faded almost away

steps.purpose: Meet the four copies, in the order they were made.

steps.title: A copy of a copy
script: Then follow the chain on the screen. Jefferson wrote a Rough Draft; others changed it, Franklin among them. The edited Fair Copy was adopted on **July 4, 1776**. The parchment with the signatures was not ordered until July 19, and most delegates signed it on **August 2**. Stone’s engraving copied the parchment.

Two surprises to finish: independence itself was decided on **July 2**; the Declaration, adopted two days later, explained a decision already made. And George Washington never signed: he was commanding the army.

screen.caption: A copy of a copy (the poster Before it was Sacred)

cells: Jefferson wrote it; Franklin and others changed it.
An edited version of the Rough Draft, adopted on July 4, 1776.
A reproduction of the Fair Copy. Ordered on July 19; most delegates signed it on August 2.
A copy of the parchment, made when the parchment was already showing its age.

steps.purpose: Follow the chain from Jefferson’s draft to the engraving.

steps.title: Which copy would you trust?
script: Ask the last question to the class: *“Which copy is the best evidence of what Congress agreed?”* There is no single right answer. The parchment is the signed original, but it is hard to read; the Dunlap broadside was printed the same night, but carries only two names; Stone’s is the clearest, but it was made forty-seven years later. Praise the reason more than the choice.

screen.question: Which copy is the best evidence of what Congress agreed in 1776? Why?

steps.purpose: Weigh the copies as evidence, with a reason.
students: Give one reason, from a clue you found.
